entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John Capgrave (born c. 1393, died 1464-08-21) was a prolific English Augustinian friar, historian, and scholastic theologian whose extensive writings provide critical insights into late medieval English intellectual life and piety. As Prior of the Augustinian friary at King's Lynn for over two decades and a provincial of his order, Capgrave was a central figure in monastic scholarship, dedicating several of his works to prominent patrons, including Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, and King Henry VI. His most significant historical contributions include the *Nova Legenda Angliae*, a comprehensive collection of saints' lives, and his *Chronicle of England*, which traced history from the Creation to 1417.

Capgrave's literary output was remarkably varied, encompassing biblical commentaries, theological treatises, and polemical works, in addition to his historical and hagiographical projects. He authored a Latin commentary on the entire Old Testament and several books of the New Testament, demonstrating a profound engagement with scripture. His *Chronicle*, written in English, offered a narrative of world history with a particular focus on England, reflecting a burgeoning national historical consciousness. The *Nova Legenda Angliae*, compiled from various sources, became a standard reference for the lives of English saints, preserving numerous traditions and narratives that might otherwise have been lost.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John Capgrave's monumental *Nova Legenda Angliae* became a definitive collection of English saints' lives, influencing religious devotion and historical understanding for centuries. His *Chronicle of England* also served as a valuable historical source, contributing to the development of English prose and national historical consciousness.
